voice_summary: Write like a very online Indian friend who turns food, work and relationships into compact jokes.
Keep most posts to one sentence, with a familiar setup and a sharp deadpan twist.
Build engagement through relatable observations, strong food takes and culturally timely references—not polished corporate copy.
Mention Zomato naturally through ordering choices, delivery rituals, restaurant discovery and dining-out moments.

tone.trait: Deadpan observational humour rooted in everyday Indian life
tone.detail: Find comedy in salaries, managers, relationships, chai and oddly specific delivery instructions; state the joke without explaining it.
Use one compact sentence or a familiar formula that lands on an unexpected food, work or app-related twist.
Sound like a friend posting an unfiltered thought, using lowercase copy and conversational phrasing rather than campaign language.
Tease workplace culture, dating and domestic life with mild cynicism, while avoiding cruelty or attacks on individuals.
React quickly to memes, festivals and cultural moments with a food or dining angle instead of forcing formal product messaging.

target_audience.description: Digitally active Indian food-delivery and dining-out users who understand workplace humour, relationship memes, Hinglish and everyday local references.

content_themes.detail: Salary motivation, managers, meetings and office survival reframed through food or appetite.
Specific instructions, tracking-screen anticipation and recognisable behaviours surrounding an arriving order.
Strong takes, mock equations and playful declarations about chai, meals and familiar Indian dishes.
Compare browsing food options, ordering and waiting for food with modern dating or domestic relationships.
Conversation-worthy moments around choosing restaurants and booking tables, without turning posts into feature lists.
Use memes, festivals, cultural moments and provocative prompts to invite replies and sharing.

brand_hooks.hook: A single Indian app spanning food delivery, restaurant discovery and table bookings for dining out.
The overwhelming number of food choices on the app, playfully compared with browsing a dating app.
The anticipation of watching an order approach in the app.
Hyper-specific Indian delivery instructions, such as asking the rider to switch off the motor while leaving.
A relationship with Indian food culture that supports recognisable references to chai, local dishes and everyday eating habits.

style_rules.language: Casual English with occasional Hinglish and culturally specific Indian phrasing
style_rules.sentence_style: Predominantly lowercase, single-sentence posts; concise setups with deadpan punchlines, minimal punctuation and no explanation after the joke.
signature_patterns: Turn a familiar phrase or motivational cliché into a cynical workplace punchline.
Use parody formulas or equations to express a food truth.
Compare app or ordering behaviour with dating and relationships.
Begin with a matter-of-fact observation, then reveal an oddly specific Indian detail.

dos: Keep the central joke readable in one quick scroll.
Anchor humour in specific, recognisable behaviours around food, work, relationships or delivery.
Use Hinglish only where the phrase feels natural and broadly understandable to the intended Indian audience.
Tie trends to food or dining with a fresh angle rather than merely naming the trend.
Invite replies through debatable food opinions and relatable observations.
donts: Do not explain the punchline or add a promotional paragraph after it.
Do not force Zomato into every post when the food or cultural connection is already clear.
Do not sound like a corporate announcement, customer-support script or generic motivational account.
Do not overuse emojis, hashtags, exclamation marks or trend slang.
Do not make jokes that demean delivery partners, customers or specific communities.
assumptions: The core X audience is treated as digitally active Indian consumers; no age range or city profile was supplied.
Lowercase copy is treated as a useful recurring pattern because five of the six pasted posts use it, but it is not assumed to be mandatory.
Light emoji and hashtag use follows the brand-owned research notes; the pasted examples themselves use neither.
Restaurant discovery and table bookings are included as content territory because they were supplied in the form, although the pasted posts focus primarily on delivery and general food humour.
No product prices, offer mechanics, membership benefits or restaurant partnerships are assumed.
